newsitem.title: USA: Sprint Q1 long-distance minutes up 14 pct.
newsitem.headline: Sprint Q1 long-distance minutes up 14 pct.

text.p: Sprint Corp said Tuesday that minutes of use on its long distance network rose 14.5 percent in the first quarter from a year earlier, while long distance revenues rose 8.5 percent, to $2.17 billion from $2.0 billion.
The company reported first quarter net earnings per share of $0.67, compared with the First Call analysts' consensus of $0.63 and the year-ago $0.77.
Local phone revenues in the quarter rose six percent, to $1.31 billion from $1.24 billion a year ago, while lines to customers increased 5.5 percent.

"We continue to believe double-digit volume, revenue and operating income growth for the full year are achievable (in the long distance market)," Art Krause, Sprint's chief financial officer, told a conference call.
Sprint noted an increase in consumer bad debt provision hindered growth in operating margins in long distance.
Those margins rose to 11.6 percent in the first quarter from 11.4 percent a year ago but were below the 11.9 percent recorded in the fourth quarter of 1996.

Krause said 1997 would be a year when Sprint would package together wireless and local calling with its long distance services, which would make the services more attractive to both new and old customers.
He predicted that the year-on-year improvement in long distance will accelerate in the second quarter from the first, because the year-ago comparisons are less challenging.
In the residential market, new customer acquisition is running ahead of a year ago, Krause said, but increased competition and bad debt continue to hinder growth in traffic volumes in that segment.
Sprint reported a 35 percent surge in revenue from wholesale traffic -- carrying traffic for other carriers.
Krause said major new contracts were won in the quarter, with Sprint now carrying long distance for four of the six regional Bells.
While this traffic is modest now, it is expected to increase sharply as regional Bells are allowed to offer long distance services to customers in their own calling regions.
Analysts say a prominent position in wholesale by long distance carriers will help to offset some of the revenue lost when regional Bells enter their markets.

Selling, general and administrative expenses fell as a percentage of revenues to 21.7 percent in the first quarter from 23.4 percent a year ago, including a 17 percent year-on-year fall in the average cost per service call handled.
